objective: Catch errors about agent memory and state.

sources.title: Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents (2025)
Anthropic docs: Handle tool calls (untrusted tool results)

followUp.question: A customer asks the agent to forget everything about them. What has to happen, and where?
rubric: delete stored memory|remove saved preferences|erase notes
scoped to the customer|per user memory|tenant scope
system of record follows its own rules|orders stay|legal retention

transfer.scenario: A coding agent works on a task for three hours and starts forgetting decisions it made early on. What do you change?
rubric: context fills up|context rot|long context degrades
clear old tool results|drop raw outputs
sub agents with clean context|split the work

narration.text: The model keeps nothing between API calls; our app sends whatever context each call needs.
Booking state, like which flights are held and what's been paid, lives in our booking database, and the agent reads it through a tool.
With a million-token window, we can keep every past conversation in the prompt, so summaries and retrieval become optional.
When a long session nears the limit, older turns are summarized and raw tool results we've already used are dropped.
The agent writes short notes, like the customer's confirmed dates, to a store outside the context, and reloads them later.
Saved preferences are scoped to the customer's account, and a deletion request removes them.
Anything the agent reads through its tools can go straight into long-term memory, because tool output is our own data.
To answer 'is my flight still held?', the agent checks the booking system rather than its notes.

planted.misconception: A large context window removes the need to manage memory.
planted.whyWrong: Every token in the window is paid for on every call and adds latency, and recall gets worse as the context grows (context rot). Past conversations also keep growing past any limit. You still choose what goes in: summaries, notes and retrieval of what's relevant.
acceptableCorrections: Even with a huge window, resending everything costs more and slows each call, and quality drops; we still summarise and retrieve what's relevant.
Select what goes into the context each time: recent turns, a summary and relevant notes.
planted.exceptions: For a short, bounded task whose full history stays small, keeping everything in context can be the simplest working choice; the error is treating window size as a memory design for open-ended history.

explain: expensive|pay every call|costs more|cost per call
quality degrades|context rot|recall drops|worse with length|lost in the middle|attention dilutes
correct: retrieve relevant|select context|relevant history|pick what matters|only relevant

planted.misconception: Tool output is trusted, so it can be saved to memory without checks.
planted.whyWrong: Tool output often carries text written by outside parties: web pages, emails, customer notes. Saving it unfiltered lets injected instructions persist and steer later sessions (memory poisoning). Write only verified facts, with their source, and keep memory scoped and reviewable.
acceptableCorrections: Treat what tools return as untrusted; only save checked facts with their source.
Filter memory writes so injected instructions from web pages can't persist.
planted.exceptions: Output from a tool that reads your own system of record (an order status) is trusted data, but it belongs in that system, not copied into memory where it goes stale.
